money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: The currency in Hong Kong is the Hong Kong Dollar (HKD). Under Hong Kong law, travellers in and out of Hong Kong may need to declare cash. Make a written declaration if you're carrying more than HKD120,000 or equivalent in cash. You can change Australian dollars for HKD at local currency exchanges and banks. Credit cards are widely accepted. Take care when using ATMs, as petty crime occurs (See 'Safety'). - Hong Kong Customs - Currency

laws.rule: Possessing illegal drugs of any kind, including marijuana, can result in penalties that include heavy fines and jail time. Officials have arrested many foreigners for trafficking drugs. Cannabidiol (CBD) has been listed as a dangerous drug under the control of the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance. Possession and consumption carries a maximum penalty of seven years imprisonment. Trafficking and illicit manufacturing of CBD carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment. From 30 April, Alternative Smoking Products (ASPs) like e-cigarettes are strictly prohibited in Hong Kong, even in transit inside the airport. Possession or use of vapes in Hong Kong can result in severe penalties including fines and
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: Strict rules control the import or possession of: any type of weapon any item that looks like a weapon, including replicas, antiques, toys and fashion accessories Hong Kong has prosecuted foreigners, including Australians, for possessing: stunning devices such as taser guns dart and spear guns knuckledusters slingshots extendable batons tear gas and pepper spray You may be able to import, possess or purchase such items legally, including from local Hong Kong markets. To do this, you must get a permit from local authorities in advance. These laws apply to people in Hong Kong and those transiting Hong Kong airport.
laws.heading: Importing weapons

laws.rule: Hong Kong has strict import rules. If you don't follow these rules, you could be fined and/or imprisoned.
laws.heading: Importing Products

laws.rule: It's illegal to: take part in public demonstrations without Hong Kong government approval take photos of military installations
laws.heading: Other laws

laws.rule: Most people in Hong Kong accept or are indifferent to LGBTQIA+ travellers. However, community attitudes towards LGBTQIA+ people are generally more conservative than in Australia. - LGBTQIA+ travellers
laws.heading: LGBTQIA+ travellers

laws.rule: For information on import restrictions for medicines and other products, see the Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department's Controlled Imports website.
laws.heading: Medications

laws.rule: You may be able to drive in Hong Kong for up to 12 months with your current Australian driver's licence (digital driver’s licences may not be accepted) or International Driving Permit (IDP). If you're residing in Hong Kong, only drive using a Hong Kong driver's licence. If you're in a car, motorcycle or bike accident, call the police to attend the site of the accident. A police report reference number will be required for insurance claims. - Hong Kong Transport Department
laws.heading: Driving permit

laws.rule: Visitors must register their small unmanned aircraft and themselves as remote pilots on CAD's eSUA portal using their travel documents, unless the flight is Standard Category A1 (aircraft up to 250 g within the operating requirements). A visitor's registration is normally valid for six months. Check the Drone Map before each flight.
laws.heading: Visitor drone registration

laws.rule: Travellers aged 18 or over can bring in 1 litre of liquor above 30% alcohol by volume without duty. Hong Kong ID card holders must have spent at least 24 hours outside Hong Kong to use the allowance.
laws.penalty_signal: Failing to declare dutiable goods over the allowance, or declaring falsely, can lead to prosecution; Customs may compound (settle by penalty) some offences.

laws.rule: The duty-free tobacco allowance for travellers aged 18 or over is one of: 19 cigarettes, or 1 cigar or 25 g of cigars, or 25 g of other manufactured tobacco.

Importing an alternative smoking product (e-cigarettes, heated tobacco products, herbal cigarettes and their parts) is prohibited, including in a traveller's luggage; personal quantities are not exempted. From 30 April 2026 no one may possess a specified alternative smoking product (capsules, heat sticks, herbal cigarettes) in a public place, and carrying an activated product counts as possession. The ban does not apply to airport transit passengers who do not clear immigration, per Customs and the Department of Health (Smartraveller's wording on transit is stricter; check before you fly).
laws.penalty_signal: Import: up to HK$500,000 (about A$90,500 at HKD 5.5234 per A$1, RBA 30 Oct 2026) and 2 years' jail on summary conviction; higher on indictment (up to 7 years). Possession in a public place, small quantities: HK$3,000 fixed penalty; otherwise prosecution (up to HK$10,000 for small quantities, HK$50,000 and 6 months for larger).

laws.rule: Pharmaceutical products and medicines need a Department of Health import licence, but a traveller's own medicines in personal baggage may be exempt if they travel with you and are a reasonable quantity for personal use. Dangerous drugs (controlled narcotics and psychotropic substances) have no personal-baggage exemption on the Customs page: they need an import licence and import certificate from the Department of Health.

tourism.detail: No visa for visits under 90 days; Hong Kong has its own immigration, separate from mainland China.

meetings.detail: Business meetings, negotiations, product presentations and signing contracts are permitted.

conference.detail: Attending short-term seminars and business meetings is permitted.

unpaid-speaking.detail: Speaking at events is permitted if you're paid nothing beyond accommodation, travel and meals, up to 14 consecutive days per stay.

paid-speaking.route: Facilitation Scheme for designated sectors, or an employment visa
paid-speaking.detail: Paid speaking is possible only through a host endorsed by the relevant government bureau, up to 14 days per arrival.
paid-speaking.next: Ask the host whether it is an endorsed organisation.

book-launch.route: Visitor (no visa needed under 90 days) if unpaid
book-launch.detail: An unpaid talk fits; selling or paid appearances are employment.
book-launch.next: Keep it to an unpaid talk, or ask the Immigration Department.

ai-teaching.route: Visitor (no visa needed under 90 days) if unpaid; the Facilitation Scheme if paid
ai-teaching.detail: Unpaid seminars fit the speaking rule; paid teaching needs the scheme or an employment visa.

remote-work.route: Not on the permissible visitor list
remote-work.detail: Visitors may not take paid or unpaid employment. The permissible activities list (meetings, seminars, exhibitions, contracts) does not mention remote work for an overseas employer.
remote-work.next: Ask the Immigration Department in writing.

sources.title: Permissible Activities for Visitors
sources.supports: list of permissible visitor business activities (read via a search-index snapshot)

entrepreneur.detail: Exploring and negotiating are permitted; starting or joining a business isn't.
entrepreneur.next: See the Immigration Department's investment routes.

trade.detail: Trade fairs, tenders and contracts are permitted; building booths or selling directly to the public isn't.
trade.next: Hire lawfully employable people for booth work.

artist.route: Facilitation Scheme or an employment visa
artist.detail: Visitors can't take employment, paid or unpaid, or start or join a business; breaching a condition of stay carries up to HK$50,000 and two years' jail.
artist.next: Ask the host whether it is an endorsed organisation.

mixed-mission.detail: The business and unpaid-speaking parts fit; any paid part needs the scheme or an employment visa.

filming.route: No general filming permit; crew may need employment entry
filming.detail: No general filming permit: notify police for public areas and get separate permission for government land, waters and private venues. Foreign crew may need work entry permits.
filming.next: Contact the Film Promotion and Facilitation Section.

sources.authority: Film Promotion and Facilitation Section, Hong Kong Government

research.route: Visitor under the short-term activities facilitation scheme (up to 14 days)
research.detail: Eligible visitors may do research, peer review and academic lectures at higher education institutions for up to 14 consecutive days per stay, without taking a local post. Longer research needs an employment or training visa.
research.next: Confirm the host institution is in the scheme.

sources.title: Immigration facilitation scheme for visitors in short-term activities

volunteering.route: Prior approval from the Director of Immigration
volunteering.detail: Visitors may not take any employment, whether paid or unpaid, without the Director of Immigration's approval, so volunteering as a visitor is not covered.
volunteering.next: Ask ImmD in writing before any volunteering.

drone-pilot-pathway.summary: CAD requires all small unmanned aircraft and remote pilots to register on eSUA, including visitors, except Standard Category A1 flights (250 g or less). Visitor registrations are normally valid for six months. Higher-risk flights and Restricted Flying Zones need prior CAD permission.

items.text: Not yet checked: no public CAD directory of drone operators was found on the pages read. CAD publishes a Drone Map of flying zones.

Remote pilot registration applies to Hong Kong residents and non-residents alike (minimum age 14), except Standard Category A1 flights of aircraft up to 250 g. Flights beyond the standard requirements or inside Restricted Flying Zones need prior CAD permission.
Visitors register through eSUA using their travel documents; a visitor's SUA registration is normally valid for six months. Pilots remain responsible for permissions from other authorities.
